To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the minimum number of sampling sites needed to monitor a large African savanna reserve (more than 1000 km2) for a single species is 4, and (2) the minimum number needed to monitor a small savanna reserve (less than 1000 km2) is 10.

(1) the minimum sampling required to reliably detect changes over 5-year periods is 1 site per 285 km in large reserves and (2) this sampling should be comprehensive in space and time, with a minimum of 1 site per reserve, 1 survey every 2 months, and a 3-year survey cycle.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the minimum level of sampling that is required to detect changes in wildlife and hunter abundance in African reserves.
the minimum sampling required to detect change, and the implications of this for monitoring programs in reserves.
the minimum level of sampling necessary to effectively monitor wildlife populations in African reserves and to identify the forces driving change in these populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the minimum sampling effort required to detect changes in wildlife population sizes is a function of the size of the reserves, the number of reserves, the number and type of species, the number of hunters and the time period over which monitoring occurs.
the minimum level of sampling necessary to reliably detect population changes over 5-year periods is 0.35% of the total area of a reserve.
the monitoring of reserves should be as comprehensive as possible.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
effective monitoring of wildlife populations in reserves is not only important, but also possible, in developing countries, even with limited resources.
the more you can sample, the more you can learn, and the less you can learn, the less you can do.
the minimum sampling required for effective monitoring of African reserves is not cheap, but it is not unreasonably expensive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
monitoring in reserves should be comprehensive, and the minimum level of sampling required is likely to be higher than many practitioners currently employ.
monitoring programs in Africa and elsewhere should be designed to maximize the information that they provide about the state of natural resources.
monitoring programs in developing countries must be designed to be comprehensive in both space and time.
